blocks.text: Where a PR day actually goes

No study we found measures how PR specialists split their hours by task. So the picture below mixes a few clear signals with general workforce data. The strongest PR-specific signal is email. O*NET's worker survey for public relations specialists found that 95% of respondents use email every day. That survey measures how often, not how long.

The job explains the rest. The Bureau of Labor Statistics lists writing press releases, preparing information for the media, responding to media requests and monitoring social media. O*NET rates updating company web sites and social media as a core task. Most of that output starts with a keyboard and a mail window.

Microsoft's data points the same way, though it covers all knowledge workers, not PR teams. Its Work Trend Index found the average employee spends 57% of their time communicating. About 43% goes to creating documents, spreadsheets and presentations. Treat these as general figures. The data runs through March 2023.

Read the chart as a map of where attention goes. Meetings and chat outrank email in Microsoft's split. For PR, though, email is where pitches, client questions and media replies arrive. The aim is not zero email. The aim is fewer minutes spent rewriting the same message.
What an AI assistant for PR specialists should do on a Mac

A useful assistant does four things. It sees what is on screen. It answers out loud, so you can ask without breaking your flow. It drafts text you can edit. It leaves the send button to you. Lazur works this way. It looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut.

items: Works in any Mac app, from Gmail in the browser to Outlook, Apple Mail, Google Docs and PowerPoint.
Points at the control you need, so you do not dig through a menu bar or ribbon.
Drafts text and types it where your cursor sits, so you edit instead of starting blank.
Keeps a memory of what you asked and did, stored on your Mac.

blocks.text: Keep the first request narrow. Ask 'Where is the attachment button in this reply?' and you get a circle and a label. Ask 'fix my week' and you get a vague answer. Narrow asks run faster. They also stop the assistant from guessing at details it cannot see.
Pitch emails: shorter, followed up, and easy to answer

Journalists are the hard audience for a pitch. Muck Rack's State of Journalism FAQ says more than half of journalists do not respond to pitch emails. The same source says 69% prefer pitches under 200 words. Write for a reader with a full inbox and little time.

Here is a worked example. A product story pitch went to a trade reporter on Monday, and nothing came back by Thursday. Open the thread in Gmail. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur where the reply box is. Then hold fn and dictate the follow-up in your own words. Keep it to a few short sentences.

Three follow-up mistakes are easy to make. The first sends a near-copy of the original pitch. The second adds a new attachment with no reason. The third asks 'Did you get my email?' Each one asks the reporter for effort. Drafting tools often lean toward 'just checking in' filler, so read every draft aloud and cut what adds nothing.
Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail on Mac: what each one does

Many PR teams use more than one mail tool. Gmail runs in your browser, so its steps are browser steps. Outlook for Mac is a desktop app. Microsoft says its features arrive in Outlook for Mac 16.58 or later. Those include Focused Inbox, shared and delegated mailboxes, and Calendar with My Day and 3-day view. Check your version under Outlook > About Outlook before you follow any steps.

blocks.text: Apple Mail has its own helpers. Apple's guide, written for macOS 27, covers Writing Tools for summarizing, proofreading and adjusting tone. It also covers signatures and junk mail. Edit your signature in Mail > Settings > Signatures. The guide does not cover snooze, schedule send or templates, so check those menus yourself.
Press releases and media kits in Google Docs and PowerPoint

A press release is writing first and layout second. Draft it in Google Docs, then gather client changes in one place. Use suggestions and comments so every change has an author. For the exact clicks, see how to [accept or reject suggestions in Google Docs](/how-to/accept-or-reject-suggestions-in-google-docs). Ask Lazur to walk you through it one click at a time.

Media kits and decks follow the same rule. Build the kit once, then reuse it. In PowerPoint on Mac, View > Slide Master is where you set fonts and logos for every slide. Ask Lazur to circle that button if you lose it. For the full walkthrough, read [PowerPoint for public relations specialists](/for/public-relations-specialists/powerpoint).
Media list research without the tab pile-up

Research gets slow when every outlet lives on a different site. Lazur can run background research in its own Chrome tabs, using the Lazur for Chrome extension. It returns a summary and a report. Give it a narrow brief, such as recent coverage of a named beat in trade titles. Then check every claim on the outlet's own site.

Cision's 2025 State of the Media report surveyed more than 3,000 journalists worldwide about their work with PR people. The page does not give pitch volumes or time use, so treat it as context, not a benchmark. When you research a writer, stick to public work details, such as a beat and a recent byline.
Client confidentiality, embargoes and regulated work

blocks.title: Check the rules first
blocks.text: Follow your agency's or employer's rules on client data and embargoed news before you put anything into an AI tool. Lazur does not replace those rules, and it does not decide what your employer allows.

Here is what Lazur does with what you say and show. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to produce an answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those are Lazur's stated terms. They are not a compliance certification.

Regulated clients add a second layer. PR for health, finance or legal clients can carry strict rules about what gets shared or published. Nurses, lawyers and other regulated staff who handle patient or client records should follow their employer's policies first. If a rule is unclear, ask your compliance team before you ask any assistant.

Embargoes are the sharpest edge. Keep the embargo time and unreleased results out of prompts unless your rules allow it. Ask Lazur for the shape of a reply, such as a headline pattern or a quote structure. Then add the sensitive facts yourself.
Slack and Gmail: keeping launch threads in order

Launch week spreads across mail and chat. Keep the media thread in Gmail and the internal sign-off in Slack, so reporters never see internal chatter. Create one channel per launch. Make it public if the wider team needs it, and private if it holds sensitive plans. The steps are in [how to create a channel in Slack](/how-to/create-a-channel-in-slack). Ask Lazur to walk you through the channel settings at your own pace.
Dictation for quotes, pitches and client notes

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Dictation is included with Lazur, and it is a quick win for PR writing. Quotes from executives, call notes and short pitch intros come out faster when you say them aloud. Read each quote back before it goes to a client, because a quote must match what was said.

Three tools help with names and repeats. Snippets hold boilerplate, such as your company description and a standard media contact line. The personal dictionary teaches the spelling of client names and product names. Clipboard slots hold items you paste often, such as a fact sheet link. Set these up before launch week, not during it.

items: Add client and product names to the personal dictionary before a launch.
Save your company boilerplate as a snippet, then check it each quarter.

blocks.text: Agency work adds a layer. If you bill several clients, keep each client's material in its own folder and its own note. Lazur keeps its memory on your Mac, so treat that memory like any other local record. Remove anything a client contract says you must not keep, and check your policy first.
How to tell if an assistant saves you time

Measure before you commit. Pick one task, such as follow-up emails. Time a handful of them this week without help, then a handful with it. Count the minutes, and count the rewrites. A saved minute that brings back a weak draft is no saving. Compare the drafts you sent, not only the drafts you wrote.
Mistakes that waste a PR morning

items: Asking for a whole press release at once. Ask for the headline, then the first paragraph, then the quote.
Pasting full client threads. Trim each one to the question and the facts you can share.
Sending the first draft. Read it aloud, cut filler, and check every name, date and figure.
Trusting background research without a check. Verify each claim on the source site.
Expecting Lazur to press buttons. It points and guides. You click send.
Waiting for Windows. Windows is planned, not available.

blocks.text: Pick one recurring task for this week. The follow-up email is a good first pick, because it repeats and it is short. Time it on Monday, then time the same task on Friday. If the drafts still need heavy edits, narrow the brief and try again.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my pitches or click the send button?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It points, explains, guides and drafts text. You review and send every message yourself.

faq.question: Is it safe to use with client material?
faq.answer: Follow your agency or employer's rules first. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those statements do not replace your employer's policy.

faq.question: Does it work in Gmail?
faq.answer: Lazur works in any app on your Mac, including Gmail in your browser. Ask it to point at a control or walk you through a menu. It does not operate Gmail for you.

faq.question: Can Lazur research journalists and outlets?
faq.answer: Yes. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension. It returns a summary and a report. Check each claim on the outlet's site before you use it in client work.

faq.question: How long is the free trial, and do I need a card?
faq.answer: Lazur offers a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. Compare the Pro and Power plans on the pricing page.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Windows is planned, not available. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with Outlook for Mac?
faq.answer: Lazur works with whatever is on your screen, so Outlook for Mac is fine. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnerships with app makers.

faq.answer: Try a follow-up email. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where the reply box is. Then hold fn and dictate a short draft. Read it aloud before you send it.

painPoints.title: Email never stops
painPoints.text: O*NET reports that 95% of PR specialists use email every day. Replies, pitches and client questions arrive in one inbox, so focus rarely lasts long.

painPoints.title: Pitches get ignored
painPoints.text: More than half of journalists do not respond to pitch emails, according to Muck Rack. Every follow-up you write has to earn its place.

painPoints.title: Writing the same thing twice
painPoints.text: Press releases, boilerplate and client updates repeat. Rewriting them by hand eats time that a fresh draft should save.

painPoints.title: Research spread over tabs
painPoints.text: Coverage, beats and outlet details live on many sites. Pulling them together by hand is slow and easy to get wrong.

painPoints.title: Confidential material in the mix
painPoints.text: Embargoes and client data sit next to routine mail. One careless paste can cause a problem you cannot undo.
